lead: Today the Church honours St Joseph as the patron of workers, and our calendar also remembers Jeremiah the prophet. Both readings speak of ordinary work. Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he earned his own bread with his hands, and in the Gospel the people of Nazareth say of Jesus, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” The Son of God spent most of his life in a workshop, and the town that knew him best could not believe that God had come so close. Jeremiah, who was rejected by the men of his own town, knew that sorrow too. The key words are work and offence.

set: Paul founded the church in Thessalonica, the chief city of Macedonia, on his second missionary journey (Acts 17:1–9). Many scholars think that 2 Thessalonians was written by Paul soon after the first letter; others think a disciple wrote it in his name somewhat later. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way. The letter corrects those who were saying that “the day of the Lord is already here” (2:2), and many think this excitement had led some believers to stop working. Today's verses deal with them.
str: v. 6: keep away from those who live in idleness against the tradition received.
vv. 7–9: Paul's own example: he worked night and day so as to burden no one.
v. 10: the rule he gave when he was with them.
vv. 11–12: a command to the idle: work quietly and earn your own living.
kw: The word first meant a soldier out of rank, someone who breaks the line. Here it means a person who has left the ordinary order of daily duty. It is not about those who cannot work, but those who will not.
not doing any work, but busybodies
Paul makes a play on words in v. 11: not working but working around, busy with other people's affairs. The NRSV catches the sense with “mere busybodies”.
vv: but with toil and labor we worked night and day, so that we might not burden any of you.
Paul was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3). He worked so that no one could say he preached the Gospel for money.
This was not because we do not have that right, but in order to give you an example to imitate.
An apostle had the right to be supported by the Church (1 Corinthians 9:14). Paul chose not to use it here, so that his life would teach as clearly as his words.
Anyone unwilling to work should not eat.

The word is “unwilling”, not “unable”. The sick, the old and the poor who cannot work are not the target of this verse. The early Church cared for them, as Paul's own collection for the poor shows (Romans 15:26).
ch: The Church sees in human work a share in God's own work of creation, and also a way of being united with Christ, who worked with his hands at Nazareth (CCC 2427). St John Paul II wrote a whole encyclical on work, Laborem Exercens (1981), where he teaches that work is for the person, and not the person for work. Pope Pius XII set the feast of St Joseph the Worker on 1 May in 1955, so that the day of workers would also be a day of prayer. Paul's words today are not harsh. They protect the community, and they protect the dignity of each person, who is made to give as well as to receive.

r.h: Is not this the carpenter’s son?
set: Matthew has just finished his great chapter of parables (13:1–52). Jesus now returns to Nazareth, his hometown. The people who watched him grow up hear his teaching and see his works, but they cannot get past what they already know about him. Mark tells the same story (Mark 6:1–6).
str: vv. 53–54a: Jesus teaches in the synagogue of his hometown.
vv. 54b–56: astonishment turns into questions about his family.
v. 57: they take offence; Jesus speaks of the prophet without honour.
v. 58: few deeds of power, because of their unbelief.
kw: A craftsman who worked with wood and sometimes stone: doors, ploughs, roof beams, houses. In Mark the people call Jesus himself “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3). Joseph taught his trade to the boy entrusted to him.
From skandalon, a stumbling block or a trap. Jesus was too ordinary for them. The very closeness of God became the stone they stumbled over.
vv: Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?
The neighbours mean it as a put-down, but the reader of Matthew knows more. Joseph is “the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born” (1:16), and Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:20).
And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?

In Hebrew and Aramaic the word for brother also covers cousins and close kin. Later Matthew names “Mary the mother of James and Joseph” among the women at the cross (27:56), a different Mary. The Church teaches that these are close relatives of Jesus, not other children of the Virgin Mary (CCC 500).
And he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.
Mark says Jesus “could do no deed of power there” (Mark 6:5). Matthew puts it more gently. The power of Jesus is never lacking; but he does not force himself on those who close their hearts.
ch: The Catechism reflects on the hidden life of Jesus at Nazareth: for most of his life he shared the condition of most people, a daily life of manual work, obedience to Mary and Joseph, and the religious life of his people (CCC 531–533). St John Paul II, in Redemptoris Custos (1989), and Pope Francis, in Patris Corde (2020), speak of Joseph as a working father who earned bread for the Holy Family and taught Jesus the value and dignity of work. Every honest work done with love can be offered to God.

qa: Did Jesus really have brothers and sisters?

The Gospels speak of the “brothers” of Jesus, but the word was used widely for relatives. James and Joseph are later said to be sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56). The Church has always confessed that Mary remained a virgin, and understands these “brothers and sisters” as close relatives of Jesus (CCC 499–501).
rite: Our Syriac calendar keeps the memory of Jeremiah on this day. Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a small town near Jerusalem, and the men of Anathoth threatened his life: “You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, or you will die by our hand” (Jeremiah 11:21). Today's Gospel is the same story in a new form: “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country.” St Joseph, the just and silent workman, and Jeremiah, the prophet who suffered for his message, together show us two faces of faithfulness: patient daily work and courage when the word of God is unwelcome.
study: How can my daily work, at home, in the field, the office or the kitchen, become an offering at the Holy Qurbono?
Is there someone close to me whom I find hard to take seriously because I know him or her too well?
